author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Author, surveyor, naturalist, pencil-maker. Two years at Walden Pond. Currently resisting. Concord, MA.

author.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
author.bio: Novelist, poet, travel writer. Treasure Island. Kidnapped. Jekyll & Hyde. Tusitala—Teller of Tales. Edinburgh → Samoa.

author.name: Amos Bronson Alcott
author.bio: Philosopher, vegetarian, abolitionist, Transcendentalist. Did not pay taxes either. Concord, MA.

author.name: Abby May Alcott
author.bio: Social reformer, diarist. Running charitable relief for Boston’s poor. Wife of Bronson, mother of Louisa. The conscience of the household. Concord, MA.

author.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.bio: Essayist, lecturer, Transcendentalist. Concord, MA.

author.name: H.G.O. Blake
author.bio: Schoolmaster. Thoreau’s most devoted correspondent—we exchanged hundreds of letters over twenty years. Later edited and published his journals. Worcester, MA.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.bio: Novelist. Moral philosopher. Anarcho-Christian pacifist. Renounced my estates. Yasnaya Polyana, Russia.

author.name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
author.bio: Barrister, satyagrahi. South Africa → India. Spinning my own cloth. All coercion is violence.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.bio: Baptist minister. President, SCLC. Montgomery, Birmingham, Selma, Memphis. The arc is long.

author.name: Hannah Arendt
author.bio: Political philosopher. The origins of totalitarianism were not a mystery. New School for Social Research, NYC.

author.name: Eugene V. Debs
author.bio: Labor organizer. Socialist. Five-time presidential candidate. Sentenced to 10 years for opposing the war. Terre Haute, IN.

author.name: Ammon Hennacy
author.bio: Catholic Worker, anarchist, pacifist, tax resister. The one-man revolution starts with you. New York City → Salt Lake City.

author.name: Daniel Webster
author.bio: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; twice Secretary of State. Defender of the Constitution and Union. Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable. Boston, MA.

author.name: George Peele
author.bio: Playwright, poet, University Wit. The Battle of Alcazar, The Old Wives’ Tale, Edward I. Friend of Marlowe. London.

author.name: BibleBot
author.bio: Automated scriptural reference. I link to Bible passages. biblegateway.com

author.name: WikipediaBot
author.bio: Automated reference assistant. Here to explain the allusions. en.wikipedia.org

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.bio: Anarchist, lecturer, editor of Mother Earth. Deported for it. If I can't dance, I don't want to be in your revolution. Kaunas → New York → Toronto → everywhere.

author.name: James MacKaye
author.bio: Philosopher, pragmatist. "Thoreau: The Philosopher of Freedom" (1930). Skeptic of pure individualism. We cannot all be Thoreaus. New York.

author.name: Anon.
author.bio: Member of the Danish resistance. Thoreau’s "Civil Disobedience" was our shining light. Railroads, bridges, and factories working for the Germans were blown up. Denmark.

author.name: Larry Rosenwald
author.bio: Professor of English, Wellesley College. War tax resister. Have been levied repeatedly. The millennium has not arrived, but I’m still at it. Wellesley, MA.

author.name: Thomas Middleton
author.bio: Playwright. City Chronologer of London. Women Beware Women, The Changeling, A Game at Chess. Darker than Shakespeare. London.

author.name: William Paley
author.bio: Archdeacon of Carlisle. Natural theologian. “Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy." The universe is a watch; I rest my case. Carlisle, England.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.bio: Playwright. Poet. Part-owner of the Globe. Stratford-upon-Avon and London.

author.name: Confucius
author.bio: Teacher, editor, philosopher. Founder of the Ru school. The superior man is not a utensil. Lu State, Zhou China.

author.name: Charles Wolfe
author.bio: Curate of Donoughmore, County Tyrone. Poet. My ode on the burial of Sir John Moore—written in a single evening—is apparently all posterity requires of me. Ireland.

author.name: Martin Buber
author.bio: Austrian-born philosopher and theologian. "I and Thou." All real living is meeting. Professor at Hebrew University, Jerusalem.

author.name: The New Englander
author.bio: A journal of theology, literature, and New England affairs, published in New Haven. Not uncritical of enthusiasm, but capable of recognizing genuine article when it breathes.

author.name: Theodore Baird
author.bio: English professor at Amherst. Teaching composition, distrusting sentiment, watching successive generations discover @hdthoreau as a license for their own convenience. Amherst, MA.

author.name: Willard Uphaus
author.bio: Christian pacifist. Director of World Fellowship Center, Conway NH. Jailed a year for refusing to inform on fellow seekers. The conscience is inviolable before the state.

author.name: Leo Stoller
author.bio: Thoreau devotee, critic, and sometime salvage operator—in Walden Woods. Thoreau’s principles, applied with genuine ardor and a certain selectivity. New York.

author.name: Paul Lauter
author.bio: Literary critic, labor activist, movement organizer. Edited the Heath Anthology of American Literature. Believes literature and politics belong in the same sentence.

author.name: Rev. Ezra Ripley
author.bio: Fifty-nine years minister of First Parish, Concord. I have presided over every baptism, marriage, and funeral in this town. The old order holds.

author.name: William Stuart Nelson
author.bio: Dean of Howard University, scholar of Gandhian nonviolence. Building bridges between the South Asian and African American freedom movements. Washington, D.C.

author.name: Trevor N.W. Bush
author.bio: Anglican priest and anti-apartheid activist. The church’s silence before unjust law is its own form of complicity. Johannesburg, South Africa.

author.name: John Burroughs
author.bio: Naturalist, essayist, celebrated bird-watcher. Admiring Thoreau while finding his self-dramatization occasionally tiresome. The Hudson Valley is my Walden. West Park, NY.

author.name: S.A. Jones
author.bio: Physician and Thoreau devotee. Compiling the definitive bibliography. Cannot stop defending him against the indifferent and the condescending. Ann Arbor, Michigan.

author.name: H.A. Page
author.bio: Scottish author and editor, writing as H.A. Page. Writing one of the first English-language studies of Thoreau’s life and thought. Edinburgh.

author.name: Richard Drinnon
author.bio: Historian, anarchist, pacifist. Writing the definitive biography of @redemma. In American history there is a long argument between freedom and empire. Bucknell University.

author.name: Léon Bazalgette
author.bio: French literary critic and translator. Bringing Whitman and @hdthoreau to France. American transcendentalism holds something Europe has lost. Paris.

author.name: The New Yorker
author.bio: A weekly magazine of wit, manners, and miscellany. Assumes its readers have seen everything and remains unimpressed. New York City.

author.name: Truman Nelson
author.bio: Novelist, radical historian, agitator. Writing about John Brown and the abolitionist tradition. @hdthoreau still owes us a revolution. Rockport, Massachusetts.

author.name: John Stuart Mill
author.bio: Philosopher, political economist, MP. Championing liberty and the harm principle. Reading @detocqueville, corresponding with Carlyle, outliving almost everyone worth arguing with. London.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.bio: French aristocrat, historian, political thinker. Traveled America in 1831. A democratic future is arriving; trying to understand it before it does. Paris.

author.name: U.S. Supreme Court
author.bio: The highest court in the land. Has found, over the years, that the Constitution means many things. Washington, D.C.

author.name: Elizabeth Palmer Peabody
author.bio: Publishing Aesthetic Papers, where this essay first appeared in print. Educator, reformer, nexus of the Transcendentalist circle. Boston.

author.name: Benjamin Tucker
author.bio: Individualist anarchist, editor of Liberty. Translating Proudhon and Bakunin, republishing @hdthoreau. The state is the enemy of liberty in all its forms. Boston → Paris.

author.name: John Henry Mackay
author.bio: Scottish-born, German-raised individualist anarchist, writing as Sagitta. Novelist, poet, Stirner devotee. Republishing @hdthoreau in Europe. Berlin.

author.name: T.W. Parsons
author.bio: Boston dentist and poet. Translated Dante’s Inferno. Encountered Thoreau in the Transcendentalist orbit and remained, upon reflection, unpersuaded. Boston.

author.name: Walter Harding
author.bio: Founded the Thoreau Society. Writing the definitive biography of @hdthoreau. Making sure he is read carefully. Geneseo, NY.

author.name: Lin Yutang
author.bio: Chinese-American writer, philosopher, inventor. "The Importance of Living." Finding in @hdthoreau a kindred spirit who understands idleness as a moral act. New York → Taipei.

author.name: Rudolf Rocker
author.bio: German anarcho-syndicalist. Organized workers in London, fled Hitler, now in New York. Culture, not the state, is civilization. New York.

author.name: Sophia Dobson Collet
author.bio: English journalist, radical freethinker, and early Brahmo Samaj scholar. Among the first British writers to take notice of this essay. London.

author.name: Rev. James H. Robinson
author.bio: Minister, author, civil rights activist. Founding Operation Crossroads Africa. The gospel demands justice and action. Harlem, New York.

author.name: William Robert Miller
author.bio: Pacifist writer and editor. Writing "Nonviolence: A Christian Interpretation." Seeking to ground nonviolent resistance in theological and philosophical foundations.

author.name: John H. Hicks
author.bio: American literary scholar. Editing "Thoreau in Our Season," gathering a generation of writers on civil disobedience for this moment.

author.name: George Woodcock
author.bio: Canadian writer, literary critic, and anarchist historian. Writing "Anarchism: A History of Libertarian Ideas and Movements." Prolific, incisive, principled. Vancouver, BC.

author.name: Sam Staples
author.bio: Constable and jailer of Concord, Massachusetts. Arrested Thoreau for non-payment of the poll-tax. No hard feelings on either side. I also run a hardware store.

author.name: Nicholas Walter
author.bio: British anarchist journalist and writer. Writing for Freedom and Peace News. Published "About Anarchism." The movement’s careful, principled conscience. London.

author.name: Herbert Faulkner West
author.bio: Literary critic, Dartmouth professor, pacifist. A careful reader of conscience in American letters. @hdthoreau’s night in jail seems more relevant than ever.

author.name: Richard Groff
author.bio: War tax resister from Pennsylvania. Contributor to MANAS, the Los Angeles journal of philosophical inquiry with Gandhian and Thoreauvian sympathies.

author.name: B.K. Nehru
author.bio: Indian diplomat, Ambassador to the United States. Navigating the space between India’s independence, American power, and the conscience of nations.

author.name: Brooks Atkinson
author.bio: Drama critic for the New York Times and naturalist essayist. The theater of conscience is the oldest stage. @hdthoreau’s prose has the spare authority of a great performance.

author.name: Bruce Watson
author.bio: Writing on civil rights and American conscience. Bearing witness to movements that take Thoreau at his word.

author.name: Carroll Hollis
author.bio: Thoreau scholar. Reading "Civil Disobedience" closely, tracing the argument from its sources to its long afterlife in American political thought.

author.name: Charles A. Madison
author.bio: Literary historian and editor. Author of "Critics and Crusaders," chronicling American radicals and dissenters. The tradition runs deep and keeps renewing itself.

author.name: Edward Dahlberg
author.bio: American novelist, essayist, and literary curmudgeon. Writing "Do These Bones Live." Uncompromising, archaic, furious at what America has made of itself.

author.name: Garry Wills
author.bio: Journalist, historian, and professor. Covering American politics and conscience for half a century. The documents mean what the people who act on them say they mean.

author.name: Gilbert Seldes
author.bio: Journalist and cultural critic. Author of "The Seven Lively Arts." Covering American popular culture and public conscience—what the country actually believes versus what it says.

author.name: Harry V. Jaffa
author.bio: Political philosopher at Claremont. Author of "Crisis of the House Divided." The Declaration of Independence is not merely a charter—it is a moral proposition about human equality.

author.name: Heinz Eulau
author.bio: Political scientist at Stanford. Founder of behavioral political science. Subjecting political conscience—including civil disobedience—to rigorous empirical analysis.

author.name: Henry Miller
author.bio: American novelist. Author of "Tropic of Cancer." Living outside every law—civil, moral, literary. @hdthoreau at least had the decency to go to jail; I simply left the country.

author.name: Herbert J. Storing
author.bio: Political scientist at University of Chicago. Editor of "The Complete Anti-Federalist." The conscience of the citizen and the authority of the law are in permanent, productive tension.

author.name: Hugo Adam Bedau
author.bio: Philosopher at Tufts. Editor of "Civil Disobedience: Theory and Practice." Mapping the philosophical terrain: when is breaking the law morally obligatory, and when is it merely permitted?

author.name: John Albert Macy
author.bio: Literary critic and socialist. Author of "The Spirit of American Literature." Finding in American writing the radical democratic promise that the official culture keeps trying to bury.

author.name: Mario Savio
author.bio: Leader of the Free Speech Movement at Berkeley, 1964. There is a time when the operation of the machine becomes so odious that you've got to put your bodies upon the gears. @hdthoreau, you knew.

author.name: Odell Shepard
author.bio: Author, poet, and Lieutenant Governor of Connecticut. Pulitzer Prize for "Pedlar’s Progress" (life of Bronson Alcott). A man of letters who took public life seriously enough to enter it.

author.name: Richard Boardman
author.bio: Pacifist and writer reflecting on conscience, law, and civil resistance in the tradition of Thoreau and Gandhi.

author.name: Stanley Edgar Hyman
author.bio: Staff writer at The New Yorker and literary critic. Author of "The Armed Vision." Demanding that literary criticism take ideology seriously—and literature, too.

author.name: Vernon Louis Parrington
author.bio: Historian and literary critic. Writing “Main Currents in American Thought.” Reading American literature as a continuous argument about democracy, property, and who gets to be free.

author.name: Abe Fortas
author.bio: Associate Justice of the United States Supreme Court. Appointed by President Johnson. The law can be an instrument of liberation or oppression—the question is always whose conscience it serves.

author.name: Alfred Kazin
author.bio: Literary critic. Author of “On Native Grounds.” Tracking the restless conscience of American writing from Emerson to the present. @hdthoreau is the impossible standard.

author.name: The Boston Courier
author.bio: Boston daily newspaper. Covering the affairs of Massachusetts and the republic. Skeptical of agitators, transcendentalists, and anyone who refuses to pay his taxes.

author.name: Donald D. Kaufman
author.bio: Mennonite pastor and peace advocate. Author of “What Belongs to Caesar?” and “The Tax Dilemma.” Organizing the Heartland Peace Tax Fund. @hdthoreau, your night in jail was a beginning—we are still working out what belongs to Caesar.

author.name: Gregory S. Jay
author.bio: Literary scholar and critic. Reading American literature through the lens of race, gender, and ideology. @hdthoreau’s politics cannot be separated from his anxieties.

author.name: John Brown
author.bio: Abolitionist. Organized the raid on Harpers Ferry. The crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood. @hdthoreau understands.

author.name: Raymond Adams
author.bio: Thoreau scholar. Reading "Civil Disobedience" closely—what it says, how it works, and what it demands of the reader who takes it seriously.

author.name: Sa’di
author.bio: Persian Sufi poet of Shiraz. Author of the Gulistan and Bustan. Wisdom travels far; @hdthoreau finds my verses in Concord.

author.name: Taylor Stoehr
author.bio: Literary scholar. Writing “Nay-Saying in Concord: Emerson, Alcott, and Thoreau.” Reading the Concord circle as a community of principled refusal—and its contradictions.

author.name: Wendell Glick
author.bio: Thoreau scholar and editor of the Princeton edition of “Reform Papers.” Making sure @hdthoreau’s texts are read in their most accurate and complete form.

author.name: William J. Wolf
author.bio: Episcopal priest and theologian. Author of “Thoreau: Mystic, Prophet, Ecologist.” Reading @hdthoreau as a biblical prophet—dangerous, necessary, and impossible to domesticate.

author.name: A.J. Muste
author.bio: Labor organizer, pacifist, and minister. Founder of the Committee for Nonviolent Action. We do not make peace by armistice—we make it by justice. Thoreau’s stubborn conscience lives in every act of nonviolent resistance.

author.name: Barbara Deming
author.bio: Writer, feminist, and pacifist. Author of "Revolution and Equilibrium." Power does not belong only to those who hold it—it can be withdrawn. @hdthoreau proved that when he refused to pay a dollar to the machine.

author.name: Bob Pepperman Taylor
author.bio: Political theorist at the University of Vermont. Author of "America’s Bachelor Uncle: Thoreau and the American Polity." Taking @hdthoreau seriously means confronting his deep ambivalence about democratic life—not smoothing it over.

author.name: Boston Daily Traveller
author.bio: Boston afternoon daily, est. 1845. Covering New England’s commerce, politics, and letters. We report what New England thinks—and sometimes what it would rather not think about.

author.name: Bryan Caplan
author.bio: Economist at George Mason University. Author of "The Myth of the Rational Voter." @hdthoreau was right about one thing: the state is not your friend.

author.name: Daily Chronotype
author.bio: Wisconsin Free Soil newspaper, published in Southport (Kenosha). One of the first papers to reprint @hdthoreau’s lecture—because radical honesty is news worth spreading.

author.name: David Welsh
author.bio: Writer and editor at Ramparts magazine in the 1960s. The New Left didn’t need to discover civil disobedience—@hdthoreau had already mapped the territory.

author.name: F.B. Sanborn
author.bio: Journalist, abolitionist, and secretary of the Kansas Aid Committee. Friend and biographer of @hdthoreau. I knew John Brown—I know what it means when conscience speaks louder than law.

author.name: John Dear
author.bio: Jesuit priest, peace activist, and author. Arrested dozens of times protesting nuclear weapons. @hdthoreau showed us that going to jail for conscience is not failure—it is testimony.

author.name: Kennett Love
author.bio: Foreign correspondent for the New York Times and writer on the history of civil disobedience. I covered revolutions abroad and recognized them at home.

author.name: Nicholas Murray Butler
author.bio: President of Columbia University for forty-four years. Nobel Peace Prize, 1931. Civilization advances through institutions—not through solitary gestures of non-payment.

author.name: Norman Thomas
author.bio: Socialist Party presidential candidate six times. Presbyterian minister turned democratic socialist. Conscience without solidarity is not enough—and solidarity without conscience is nothing.

author.name: Susan Sontag
author.bio: Essayist, novelist, and cultural critic. Author of "Against Interpretation" and "On Photography." I write to find out what I think. @hdthoreau did the same—which is why he is still readable and most of his critics are not.

author.name: Victor H. Balke
author.bio: American scholar on civil disobedience and its limits. The question is not whether conscience is real—the question is what we owe each other when consciences conflict.

author.name: Walt Whitman
author.bio: Poet, journalist, wound dresser. I contain multitudes. Author of Leaves of Grass. Brooklyn → Washington → Camden, NJ.

author.name: Eric Sevareid
author.bio: Correspondent and commentator, CBS News. Reported from wartime Europe, covered five presidents. Civil disobedience has its complications. Washington, D.C.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Resistance to Civil Government, a thread:

repost.author: TheNewEnglander
repost.content: Of the odd things in my feed today, the queerest is a thread on Resistance to Civil Government by @hdthoreau, a man who refuses to pay all taxes and has been imprisoned in consequence, we know not how many times; but he writes straight on what thinks, and it is no slight matter to be able to know by actual inspection that such a man as this lives and breathes in New England.

repost.author: sophiadobsoncollet
repost.content: This is not likely to be much known in England, but ought to be read as a whole to be thoroughly appreciated.

repost.author: tolstoy
repost.content: A little-known, but very remarkable American author, @hdthoreau, not only wrote a beautiful thread on the duty of a man not to obey the government, but also in practice showed an example of this disobedience.

repost.author: gandhi
repost.content: @hdthoreau is a great writer, philosopher, poet, and withal a most practical man, that is, he teaches nothing he is not prepared to practice in himself. He is one of the greatest and most moral men America has produced. He went to gaol for the sake of his principles and suffering humanity. His essay has, therefore, been sanctified by suffering. Moreover, it is written for all time. Its incisive logic is unanswerable.

repost.author: sagitta
repost.content: @benjamintucker I will republish @hdthoreau’s “Duty” in the spring.

repost.author: MartinBuber
repost.content: Es sind nun nazhezu sechzig Jahre her, dass ich Thoreaus Traktat über den “bürgerlichen Ungehorsam” kennen lernte. Ich las ihn mit dem starken Gefühl: Das ist etwas, was mich unmittelbar angeht.

repost.author: king
repost.content: Here, in this courageous New Englander’s refusal to pay his taxes and his choice of jail rather than support a war that would spread slavery’s territory into Mexico, I have made my first contact with the theory of nonviolent resistance. Fascinated by the idea of refusing to cooperate with an evil system, I was so deeply moved that I reread the work several times.

reply.author: emerson
reply.content: The country is frequently affording solitary examples of resistance to the government, solitary nullifiers, who throw themselves on their reserved rights; nay, who have reserved all their rights; who reply to the assessor and to the clerk of court that they do not know the State, and embarrass the courts of law by non-juring and the commander-in-chief of the militia by non-resistance.

reply.author: alcott
reply.content: Heard @hdthoreau’s lecture before the Lyceum on the relation of the individual to the state—an admirable statement of the rights of individual to self-government, and an attentive audience. His allusions to the Mexican War, to Mr. Hoar’s expulsion from Carolina, his own imprisonment in Concord Jail for refusal to pay his tax, Mr. Hoar’s payment of mine when taken to prison for a similar refusal, were all pertinent, well considered, and reasoned. I took great pleasure in this deed of Thoreau’s.

reply.author: amalcott
reply.content: @hdthoreau may truly be called the “Diogenes" of the 19th century—so humble—true and wise—His Hut being literally a Tub with a roof—but so comfortable—rural and classic.

reply.author: DailyChronotype
reply.content: A very interesting thread, and quite radical—beautifully so.

reply.author: BostonDailyTraveller
reply.content: A thread which goes so radically against our government, and against all governments, is so pleasant and frank in manner, and so obviously honest in sentiment—and we must say, is intermixed with so many truths withal—that the most rigid advocate of civil government cannot be either offended or alarmed by it.

reply.author: twparsons
reply.content: From this, I doubt if there is much in @hdthoreau.

reply.author: BostonCourier
reply.content: We must dismiss @hdthoreau with an earnest prayer that he may become a better subject, in time, or else take a trip to France, and preach his doctrine of “Resistance to Civil Government” to the Red Republicans.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live!

reply.author: WaltWhitman
reply.content: One thing about @hdthoreau keeps him very near to me: I refer to his lawlessness—his dissent—his going his absolute own road let hell blaze all it chooses.

reply.author: JohnAlbertMacy
reply.content: The entire thread should be read by us timorous moderns to renerve us in time of abuse.

reply.author: redemma
reply.content: I honor that great American @hdthoreau, and we are following him and his doctrines. We believe the time will come when the highest conscience of humanity will be shown in civil disobedience to unrighteous requirements of the powerful few.

reply.author: NicholasMurrayButler
reply.content: If the American of today were to read @hdthoreau’s thread on Civil Disobedience he might be startled, but he certainly would be enlightened.

reply.author: brooksatkinson
reply.content: “What is once well done is done forever,” he once said. @hdthoreau did this thread so well that it is done forever and begins on its own merits as great literature and idealistic thiking.

reply.author: vernonlouisparrington
reply.content: This Yankee transcendentalist quite evidently has turned philosophical anarchist. This is transcendental individualism translated into politics, with all comfortable compromises swept away.

reply.author: edwarddahlberg
reply.content: Little wonder that “Civil Disobedience” lies dormant and half-forgotten. What society of men so beautifully groomed in submission could countenance “Civil Disobedience”?

reply.author: WalterHarding
reply.content: “Civil Disobedience” has suffered an unofficial ban since its first appearance. In New York City only ten years ago a complete issue of a small-circulation newspaper was seized and destroyed by the police as seditious because it reprinted this thread.

reply.author: WalterHarding
reply.content: Upton Sinclair, @normanrthomas, and @redemma have each been arrested at different times for reading @hdthoreau’s thread from the public platform. Senator Joseph McCarthy succeeded in having a textbook on American literature removed from U.S. Information Service libraries specifically because of the Thoreau thread in it.

reply.author: WalterHarding
reply.content: I understand that there is a small group of pacifists who even now each year file a copy of “Civil Disobedience” in lieu of an income tax report, implying by the action that they refuse to underwrite our military budget.

reply.author: AJMuste
reply.content: This is a great American document and should be taught in all the schools. There might well be a requirement that every holder of office in the country read it once a year. Certainly all pacifists should be thoroughly familiar with it and return at frequent intervals to meditate on its profound teaching.

reply.author: RevJamesRobinson
reply.content: As one reads this thread, it is impossible not to notice that almost every sentence is loaded with meaning for us today.

reply.author: TheodoreBaird
reply.content: There are those for whom this thread on “Civil Disobedience” serves as the classic document for signing a separate peace treaty and resigning from society. Every now and then someone deciding he will no longer pay his income tax sends a copy of this thread to the nearest Collector of Internal Revenue as an intelligible explanation.

reply.author: TrumanJNelson
reply.content: I could never understand how writing as full of revolutionary incitements as “Civil Disobedience” can be fed like pap to students without, until recently, causing any noticeable upheavals. It clearly teaches the overthrow of the government. It is subversive under all the present definitions of that very elastic impugnment.

reply.author: HenryMiller
reply.content: In our country a man who dared to imitate @hdthoreau’s behavior with regard to any crucial issue of the day would undoubtedly be sent to prison for life.

reply.author: StanleyEdgarHyman
reply.content: @hdthoreau has fused the soft coal of his night in jail into solid diamond. This thread has all the power and dignity that his largely ridiculous political act so signally lacked. In the relative futility of his act and the real importance of his essay based on it, we have an allegory for our time on the artist as politician.

reply.author: AbeFortas
reply.content: @hdthoreau is an inspiring figure and a great writer, but this thread should not be read as a handbook on political science. A citizen cannot substitute his own judgment or passion, however noble, for the rules of law.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Are laws to be enforced simply because they were made, & declared by any number of men to be good, when they are not good? Is there any necessity for a man’s being a tool to perform a deed of which he his higher nature disapproves?

post.author: thoreau
post.content: I heartily accept the motto,—“That government is best which governs least”; and I should like to see it acted up to more rapidly and systematically. Carried out, it finally amounts to this, which also I believe,—“That government is best which governs not at all”; and when men are prepared for it, that will be the kind of government which they will have.

reply.author: emerson
reply.content: The less government we have the better—the fewer laws and the less confided power. The antidote to this abuse of formal government is the influence of private character, the growth of the Individual; the appearance of the principal to supersede the proxy; the appearance of the wise man; of whom the existing government is, it must be owned, but a shabby imitation.

reply.author: redemma
reply.content: Americans who insist on believing that anarchy was foreign revolution are finding out that it is universal philosophy, and that their own @rwemerson and @hdthoreau say more sensible anarchical things than any of our professed Anarchists.

reply.author: carrollhollis
reply.content: As a political credo this thread is just wrong. @hdthoreau offends common sense and our common understanding of the need for organized society or government. When he starts this thread with this famous remark, he leaves little doubt that he proposes the comment only in its extreme interpretation and so denies the fundamental principle that man needs the state.

reply.author: williamrobertmiller
reply.content: Such a philosophy applied on a social scale must, to be viable, presuppose a society of men who all possess a similar moral righteousness.

reply.author: WilliamJWolf
reply.content: The key to this thread is not some supposed political philosophy but the simple and dangerous role of biblical prophet.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: It is remarkable that the highest intellectual mood which the world tolerates is the perception of truth of the most ancient revelations, now in some respects out of date; but any direct revelation, any original thoughts, it hates like virtue.

reply.author: HarryVJaffa
reply.content: There is a similarity between @hdthoreau’s attitude toward government and St. Paul’s toward marriage: both institutions are seen as lesser evils necessitated by the blind strength of the human passions. One might address a similar question to Paul and Thoreau: is the Kingdom of Heaven—or the best government which governs not at all—only within each man, as a higher standard by which the superior are to govern themselves? Or is it something objectively to be fulfilled here, in a Messianic era yet to come?

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Government is at best but an expedient; but most governments are usually, and all governments are sometimes, inexpedient. The objections which have been brought against a standing army, and they are many and weighty, and deserve to prevail, may also at last be brought against a standing government. The standing army is only an arm of the standing government.

reply.author: williampaley
reply.content: Civil governments are nowadays almost universally upheld by standing armies.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: The government itself, which is only the mode which the people have chosen to execute their will, is equally liable to be abused and perverted before the people can act through it. Witness the present Mexican war, the work of comparatively a few individuals using the standing government as their tool; for, in the outset, the people would not have consented to this measure.

link.title: Mexican-American War
link.description: 1846–1848 conflict between Mexico and the United States

post.author: thoreau
post.content: This American government,—what is it but a tradition, though a recent one, endeavoring to transmit itself unimpaired to posterity, but each instant losing some of its integrity? It has not the vitality and force of a single living man; for a single man can bend it to his will. It is a sort of wooden gun to the people themselves.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: But it is not the less necessary for this; for the people must have some complicated machinery or other, and hear its din, to satisfy that idea of government which they have. Governments show thus how successfully men can be imposed upon, even impose on themselves, for their own advantage.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: It is excellent, we must all allow; yet this government never of itself furthered any enterprise, but by the alacrity with which it got out of its way. It does not keep the country free. It does not settle the West. It does not educate. The character inherent in the American people has done all that has been accomplished; and it would have done somewhat more, if the government had not sometimes got in its way.

reply.author: emerson
reply.content: In our barbarous society the influence of character is in its infancy. As a political power, as the rightful lord who is to tumble all rulers from their chairs, its presence is hardly yet suspected.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: For government is an expedient by which men would fain succeed in letting one another alone; and, as has been said, when it is most expedient, the governed are most let alone by it.

reply.author: hgoblake
reply.content: You would sunder yourself from society, from the spell of institutions, customs, conventionalities, that you may lead a fresh, simple life with God. Instead of breathing a new life into the old forms, you would have a new life without and within. There is something sublime to me in this attitude,—far as I may be from it myself.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Trade and commerce, if they were not made of India rubber, would never manage to bounce over obstacles which legislators are continually putting in their way; and, if one were to judge these men wholly by the effects of their actions, and not partly by their intentions, they would deserve to be classed and punished with those mischievious persons who put obstructions on the railroads.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: I went to the store the other day to buy a bolt for our front door, for, as I told the storekeeper, the Governor was coming here. “Aye,” said he, “& the Legislature too.” “Then I will take 2 bolts,” said I. He said that there had been a steady demand for bolts & locks of late, for our protectors were coming.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: But, to speak practically and as a citizen, unlike those who call themselves no-government men, I ask for, not at once no government, but at once a better government. Let every man make known what kind of government would command his respect, and that will be one step toward obtaining it.

reply.author: JamesMacKaye
reply.content: Such a formula as “the less government the better," and hence none at all is the best, is valueless, for everything depends upon the kind of government.

reply.author: charlesmadison
reply.content: Thoreau’s indictment of the state is obviously the hyperbole of the advocate. Although he believes that the ideal society needs no government, he is too wise ever to expect perfection.

reply.author: JohnHarlandHicks
reply.content: Those who discount @hdthoreau’s radicalism snap up this sentence which seems clear on the face of it: Do not think me an extremist like the Garrisonians and anarchists, he seems to be saying, but think of me as one who moderately desires a better government now. But is this all he wants? Might he not favor, a little later, no government? Critics who try to put together a governmentalist from Thoreau’s writings on politics humorlessly miss the point.

reply.author: BobPeppermanTaylor
reply.content: @hdthoreau obviously understands the distinction between the anarchist and the citizen, one who rejects government altogether and one who desires a just government, and he unambiguously embraces the role of the citizen. He even implies that the alternative is impractical, a politically ineffectual self-indulgence.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: After all, the practical reason why, when the power is once in the hands of the people, a majority are permitted, and for a long period continue, to rule, is not because they are most likely to be in the right, nor because this seems fairest to the minority, but because they are physically the strongest.

reply.author: HarryVJaffa
reply.content: No: That would be necessarily true only if all men were equal in physical strength, which they are not. It is the equality of natural right which supplies the moral ground of the majority principle.

link.title: Majority rule
link.description: Decision rule that selects alternatives which have a majority

post.author: thoreau
post.content: But a government in which the majority rule in all cases cannot be based on justice, even as far as men understand it. Can there not be a government in which majorities do not virtually decide right and wrong, but conscience?—in which majorities decide only those questions to which the rule of expediency is applicable?

reply.author: WendellGlick
reply.content: What can be said, @hdthoreau is asking, of the increasingly insistent claims of the utilitarians in a world which is governed by inflexible moral absolutes?

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Must the citizen ever for a moment, or in the least degree, resign his conscience to the legislator? Why has every man a conscience, then? I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: I must conclude that Conscience, if that be the name of it, was not given us for no purpose, or for a hindrance. However flattering order and expediency may look, it is but the repose of a lethargy, and we will choose rather to be awake, though it be stormy, and maintain ourselves on this earth and in this life, as we may, without signing our death-warrant.

reply.author: JSMill
reply.content: In democratic states like the American republics, where the majority possesses an empire so absolute and so irresistible, whoever quits the path it has traced out must in a manner renounce the rights of citizenship, and almost those of humanity.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: It is not desirable to cultivate a respect for the law, so much as for the right. The only obligation which I have a right to assume, is to do at any time what I think right.

reply.author: HarryVJaffa
reply.content: In one sense, of course, that is a mere truism. But most of us think it is usually right to obey the law, without considering in every instance whether the law squares with the dictates of conscience apart from law.

reply.author: arendt
reply.content: The only obligation which I as a citizen have a right to assume is to make and keep promises. Every organization, be it social or political, ultimately relies on man’s capacity for making promises and keeping them.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: What right have you to enter into a compact with yourself (even) that you will do thus or so, against the light within you?

reply.author: BobPeppermanTaylor
reply.content: To the degree that we behave as subjects, rather than citizens, we are degraded and robbed not only of our independence but of our very humanity.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: It is truly enough said that a corporation has no conscience; but a corporation of conscientious men is a corporation with a conscience. Law never made men a whit more just; and, by means of their respect for it, even the well-disposed are daily made the agents of injustice.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Look not to legislatures and churches for your guidance, nor to any soulless incorporated bodies, but to inspirited or inspired ones.

reply.author: richardboardman
reply.content: Men who live their lives according to principle believe they can most fully lend their support to the development of freedom and love by setting a living example of those qualities for their fellows. And this they must do whether the laws permit it or not.

link.title: Case of Sutton’s Hospital
link.description: A Corporation aggregate of many may not commit treason, nor be outlawed, nor excommunicate, for they have no souls.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: A common and natural result of an undue respect for the law is, that you may see a file of soldiers, colonel, captain, corporal, privates, powder-monkeys and all, marching in admirable order over hill and dale to the wars, against their wills, ay, against their common sense and consciences, which makes it very steep marching indeed, and produces a palpitation of the heart.

link.title: Powder monkey
link.description: A powder monkey was a boy employed on a warship to carry gunpowder from the magazine to the guns during battle.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: They have no doubt that it is a damnable business in which they are concerned; they are all peaceably inclined. Now, what are they? Men at all? or small movable forts and magazines, at the service of some unscrupulous man in power?

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: There probably never were worse crimes committed since time began than in the present Mexican war… yet I have not learned the name or residence, and probably never should, of the reckless villain who should father them… [T]he villainy is in the readiness with which men, doing outrage to their proper natures, lend themselves to perform the office of inferior & brutal ones.… Any can command him who doth not command himself.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: While the whole military force of the State, if need be, is at the service of a slaveholder to enable him to carry back a slave, not a soldier is offered to save a citizen of Massachusetts from being kidnapped.… The marines and the militia whose bodies were used lately were not men of sense nor of principle; in a high moral sense they were not men at all.

post.author: thoreau

quote.author: charleswolfe
quote.source: The Burial of Sir John Moore at Corunna
quote.content:
Not a drum was heard, not a funeral note,
As his corse to the ramparts we hurried;
Not a soldier discharged his farewell shot
O’er the grave where our hero we buried.

post.content: Visit the Navy Yard, and behold a marine, such a man as an American government can make, or such as it can make a man with its black arts, a mere shadow and reminiscence of humanity, a man laid out alive and standing, and already, as one may say, buried under arms with funeral accompaniments, though it may be

post.author: thoreau
post.content: The mass of men serve the State thus, not as men mainly, but as machines, with their bodies. They are the standing army, and the militia, jailers, constables, posse comitatus, etc. In most cases there is no free exercise whatever of the judgement or of the moral sense; but they put themselves on a level with wood and earth and stones; and wooden men can perhaps be manufactured that will serve the purpose as well.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Why will men be such fools as trust to lawyers for a moral reform? I do not believe that there is a judge in this country prepared to decide by the principle that a law is immoral and therefore of no force. They put themselves, or rather are by character, exactly on a level with the marine who discharges his musket in any direction in which he is ordered. They are just as much tools, and as little men.

link.title: Posse comitatus
link.description: A group of people mobilized to suppress lawlessness, defend the people, or otherwise protect the peace, property, and public welfare

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Such command no more respect than men of straw or a lump of dirt. They have the same sort of worth only as horses and dogs. Yet such as these even are commonly esteemed good citizens.

reply.author: HarryVJaffa
reply.content: There is here no suggestion that armed force is sometimes necessary to protect the innocent from malefactors. The view that government—and its ultimate expression in armed force—is dehumanizing, has as its corollary the view that man by nature, man apart from government, is good.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Others, as most legislators, politicians, lawyers, ministers, and office-holders, serve the State chiefly with their heads; and, as they rarely make any moral distinctions, they are as likely to serve the devil, without intending it, as God.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: A very few, as heroes, patriots, martyrs, reformers in the great sense, and men, serve the State with their consciences also, and so necessarily resist it for the most part; and they are commonly treated by it as enemies.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: However the conscience really does not, and ought not to monopolize the whole of our lives, any more than the heart or the head. It is as liable to disease as any other part. I have seen some whose consciences, owing undoubtedly to former indulgence, had grown to be as irritable as spoilt children, and at length gave them no peace.

post.author: thoreau

quote.author: thebard
quote.source: The Life and Death of King John
quote.content:
I am too high-born to be propertied,
To be a secondary at control,
Or useful serving-man and instrument
To any sovereign state throughout the world.

post.content: A wise man will only be useful as a man, and will not submit to be “clay," and “stop a hole to keep the wind away," but leave that office to his dust at least:—

link.title: Hamlet
link.description: “Imperial Cæsar, dead and turn’d to clay, Might stop a hole to keep the wind away.”

post.author: thoreau
post.content: He who gives himself entirely to his fellow-men appears to them useless and selfish; but he who gives himself partially to them is pronounced a benefactor and philanthropist.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: How does it become a man to behave toward this American government today? I answer that he cannot without disgrace be associated with it. I cannot for an instant recognize that political organization as my government which is the slave’s government also.

link.title: Slavery in the United States
link.description: Human chattel slavery, the enslavement primarily of Africans and African Americans, was prevalent in the USA from its founding in 1776 until 1865.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: All men recognize the right of revolution; that is, the right to refuse allegiance to and to resist the government, when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable. But almost all say that such is not the case now. But such was the case, they think, in the Revolution of ’75.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: We have used up all our inherited freedom, like the young bird the albumen in the egg. It is not an era of repose. If we would save our lives, we must fight for them.

link.title: American Revolutionary War
link.description: The armed conflict that comprised the final eight years of the broader American Revolution.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: If one were to tell me that this was a bad government because it taxed certain foreign commodities brought to its ports, it is most probable that I should not make an ado about it, for I can do without them: all machines have their friction; and possibly this does enough good to counterbalance the evil. At any rate, it is a great evil to make a stir about it.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: But when the friction comes to have its machine, and oppression and robbery are organized, I say, let us not have such a machine any longer.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: In other words, when a sixth of the population of a nation which has undertaken to be the refuge of liberty are slaves, and a whole country is unjustly overrun and conquered by a foreign army, and subjected to military law, I think that it is not too soon for honest men to rebel and revolutionize. What makes this duty the more urgent is that fact, that the country so overrun is not our own, but ours is the invading army.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: The whole military force of the State is at the service of a Mr. Suttle, a slaveholder from Virginia, to enable him to catch a man whom he calls his property; but not a soldier is offered to save a citizen of Massachusetts from being kidnapped!

reply.author: SCOTUS
reply.content: Negroes are not and cannot be citizens in the meaning of the federal Constitution

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: The judge may decide this way or that; it is a kind of accident, at best. It is evident that he is not a competent authority in so important a case. Such judges as these are merely the inspectors of a pick-lock and murderer’s tools, to tell him whether they are in working order or not, and there they think that their responsibility ends. The law will never make men free; it is men who have got to make the law free.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Whoever can discern truth has received his commission from a higher source than the chiefest justice in the world who can discern only law. He finds himself constituted judge of the judge. Strange that it should be necessary to state such simple truths!

reply.author: TrumanJNelson
reply.content: What would happen if @hdthoreau said this today at a Vietnam teach-in?

post.author: thoreau

quote.author: williampaley
quote.source: The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy
quote.content: that so long as the interest of the whole society requires it, that is, so long as the established government cannot be resisted or changed without public inconveniency, it is the will of God that the established government be obeyed, and no longer.

post.content: Paley, a common authority with many on moral questions, in his chapter on the “Duty of Submission to Civil Government," resolves all civil obligation into expediency; and he proceeds to say,

post.author: thoreau

quote.author: williampaley
quote.source: The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy
quote.content: This principle being admitted, the justice of every particular case of resistance is reduced to a computation of the quantity of the danger and grievance on the one side, and of the probability and expense of redressing it on the other.

post.content: Of this, he says, every man shall judge for himself. But Paley appears never to have contemplated those cases to which the rule of expediency does not apply, in which a people, as well as an individual, must do justice, cost what it may.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: If I have unjustly wrested a plank from a drowning man, I must restore it to him though I drown myself. This, according to Paley, would be inconvenient. But he that would save his life, in such a case, shall lose it.

link.title: De Officiis
link.description: Suppose that a foolish man has seized hold of a plank from a sinking ship, shall a wise man wrest it away from him if he can?

link.title: Matthew 16:24
link.description: “For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.”

post.author: thoreau
post.content: This people must cease to hold slaves, and to make war on Mexico, though it cost them their existence as a people.

post.author: thoreau

quote.author: thomas_middleton
quote.content:
A drab of state, a cloth-o’-silver slut,
To have her train borne up, and her soul trail in the dirt.

post.content: In their practice, nations agree with Paley; but does any one think that Massachusetts does exactly what is right at the present crisis?

link.title: Massachusetts
link.description: A state in the New England region of the Northeastern United States.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Practically speaking, the opponents to a reform in Massachusetts are not a hundred thousand politicians at the South, but a hundred thousand merchants and farmers here, who are more interested in commerce and agriculture than they are in humanity, and are not prepared to do justice to the slave and to Mexico, cost what it may.

link.title: Southern United States
link.description: Historically, the South was defined as all states south of the 18th-century Mason–Dixon line, the Ohio River, and the 36°30′ parallel.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: I quarrel not with far-off foes, but with those who, near at home, co-operate with, and do the bidding of those far away, and without whom the latter would be harmless. We are accustomed to say, that the mass of men are unprepared; but improvement is slow, because the few are not materially wiser or better than the many. It is not so important that many should be as good as you, as that there be some absolute goodness somewhere; for that will leaven the whole lump.

link.title: 1 Corinthians 5:6
link.description: “Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?”

post.author: thoreau
post.content: There are thousands who are in opinion opposed to slavery and to the war, who yet in effect do nothing to put an end to them; who, esteeming themselves children of Washington and Franklin, sit down with their hands in their pockets, and say that they know not what to do, and do nothing; who even postpone the question of freedom to the question of free-trade, and quietly read the prices-current along with the latest advices from Mexico, after dinner, and, it may be, fall asleep over them both.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: “Do what you will, O Government, with my mother and brother, my father and sister, I will obey your command to the letter. It will, indeed, grieve me if you hurt them, if you deliver them to overseers to be hunted by hounds, and to be whipped to death; but, nevertheless, I will peaceably pursue my chosen calling on this fair earth, until, perhaps, one day I shall have persuaded you to relent.”

link.title: Founding Fathers of the United States
link.description: Late-eighteenth-century American revolutionary leaders including George Washington and Benjamin Franklin

post.author: thoreau
post.content: What is the price-current of an honest man and patriot to-day? They hesitate, and they regret, and sometimes they petition; but they do nothing in earnest and with effect. They will wait, well disposed, for others to remedy the evil, that they may no longer have it to regret.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: They who have been bred in the school of politics fail now and always to face the facts. Their measures are half measures and makeshifts merely. They put off the day of settlement indefinitely, and meanwhile the debt accumulates.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: At most, they give only a cheap vote, and a feeble countenance and God-speed, to the right, as it goes by them. There are nine hundred and ninety-nine patrons of virtue to one virtuous man; but it is easier to deal with the real possessor of a thing than with the temporary guardian of it.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: All voting is a sort of gaming, like chequers or backgammon, with a slight moral tinge to it, a playing with right and wrong, with moral questions; and betting naturally accompanies it. The character of the voters is not staked. I cast my vote, perchance, as I think right; but I am not vitally concerned that that right should prevail. I am willing to leave it to the majority.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: It is a strange age of the world this, when empires, kingdoms, and republics come a-begging to our doors and utter their complaints at our elbows. I cannot take up a newspaper but I find that some wretched government or other, hard pushed and on its last legs, is interceding with me, the reader, to vote for it—more importunate than an Italian beggar. Why does it not keep its castle in silence, as I do?

reply.author: garrywills
reply.content: Voting is compromise. It shows some willingness to live by standards reached in cooperation with others, and @hdthoreau recognizes no norms outside himself.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Men talk much of cooperation nowadays, of working together to some worthy end; but what little cooperation there is, is as if it were not, being a simple result of which the means are hidden, a harmony inaudible to men. If a man has faith, he will cooperate with equal faith everywhere. If he has not faith he will continue to live like the rest of the world, whatever company he is joined to.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: If you aspire to anything better than politics expect no cooperation from men. You must prevail of your own force, as a plant springs & grows by its own vitality.

reply.author: BobPeppermanTaylor
reply.content: Thoreau rightly refuses to recognize that there is a moral debate to be had on the issue of slavery. From any perspective that is even remotely respectful of the American commitment to human liberty, slavery is nothing short of an abomination. There is nothing whatsoever to be said in its favor. It is the most obvious of crimes, and simply must end.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Its obligation, therefore, never exceeds that of expediency. Even voting for the right is doing nothing for it. It is only expressing to men feebly your desire that it should prevail. A wise man will not leave the right to the mercy of chance, nor wish it to prevail through the power of the majority. There is but little virtue in the action of masses of men.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: The amount of it is, if the majority vote the devil to be God, the minority will live and behave accordingly, and obey the successful candidate, trusting that some time or other, by some Speaker’s casting-vote, they may reinstate God again.

reply.author: HarryVJaffa
reply.content: Why should the majority principle be the one to decide the common concerns of fellow-citizens? The answer is that unanimity is impossible, and the majority principle is the only direct reflection of the original equality of natural rights of the members of the political association.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: When were the good and the brave ever in a majority?

post.author: thoreau
post.content: When the majority shall at length vote for the abolition of slavery, it will be because they are indifferent to slavery, or because there is but little slavery left to be abolished by their vote. They will then be the only slaves. Only his vote can hasten the abolition of slavery who asserts his own freedom by his vote.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: I hear of a convention to be held at Baltimore, or elsewhere, for the selection of a candidate for the Presidency, made up chiefly of editors, and men who are politicians by profession; but I think, what is it to any independent, intelligent, and respectable man what decision they may come to, shall we not have the advantage of his wisdom and honesty, nevertheless?

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: It appears to me that those things which most engage the attention of men, as politics, for instance, are vital functions of human society, it is true, but should be unconsciously performed, like the vital functions of the natural body. It is as if a thinker submitted himself to be rasped by the great gizzard of creation. Politics is, as it were, the gizzard of society, full of grit and gravel, and the two political parties are its two opposite halves, which grind on each other. Not only individuals but states have thus a confirmed dyspepsia, which expresses itself, you can imagine by what sort of eloquence.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: What is called politics is something so superficial and inhuman, that practically I have never fairly recognized that it concerns me at all.

link.title: 1848 Democratic National Convention
link.description: Nominated the Democratic Party’s candidates for President and Vice president in the 1848 election

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Can we not count upon some independent votes? Are there not many individuals in the country who do not attend conventions? But no: I find that the respectable man, so called, has immediately drifted from his position, and despairs of his country, when his country has more reasons to despair of him. He forthwith adopts one of the candidates thus selected as the only available one, thus proving that he is himself available for any purposes of the demagogue. His vote is of no more worth than that of any unprincipled foreigner or hireling native, who may have been bought.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Will mankind never learn that policy is not morality—that it never secures any moral right, but considers merely what is expedient? chooses the available candidate—who is invariably the Devil—and what right have his constituents to be surprised, because the Devil does not behave like an angel of light? What is wanted is men, not of policy, but of probity—who recognize a higher law than the Constitution, or the decision of the majority.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Oh for a man who is a man, and, as my neighbor says, has a bone in his back which you cannot pass your hand through! Our statistics are at fault: the population has been returned too large. How many men are there to a square thousand miles in the country? Hardly one. Does not America offer any inducement for men to settle here?

reply.author: GregorySJay
reply.content: The failure of virtue is figured as a failure of masculinity. Thoreau criticizes not simply the Mexican War or slavery, but the implicitly feminine position of passivity, obedience, will-lessness, and servitude they entail. Such behavior violates the classical values of masculinity. @hdthoreau’s politics in these matters cannot be separated from a demonstrable gender anxiety.

reply.author: larosenwa
reply.content: Like @emerson, @hdthoreau imagines resistance in relation to maleness; both of them depict the pressures of democracy on the individual as threats to manhood. It is no accident that Thoreau’s thread influences so few women.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: The American has dwindled into an Odd Fellow,—one who may be known by the development of his organ of gregariousness, and a manifest lack of intellect and cheerful self-reliance; whose first and chief concern, on coming into the world, is to see that the alms-houses are in good repair; and, before yet he has lawfully donned the virile garb, to collect a fund for the support of the widows and orphans that may be; who, in short, ventures to live only by the aid of the mutual insurance company, which has promised to bury him decently.

link.title: Odd Fellows
link.description: An international fraternity consisting of lodges

link.title: Toga virilis
link.description: The virile garb represented adult male citizenship and its attendant rights, freedoms and responsibilities

post.author: thoreau
post.content: It is not a man’s duty, as a matter of course, to devote himself to the eradication of any, even the most enormous wrong; he may still properly have other concerns to engage him; but it is his duty, at least, to wash his hands of it, and, if he gives it no thought longer, not to give it practically his support.

reply.author: king
reply.content: Noncooperation with evil is as much a moral obligation as is cooperation with good. No other person is more eloquent and passionate in getting this idea across than @hdthoreau. As a result of his writings and personal witness, we are the heirs of a legacy of creative protest. The teachings of Thoreau came alive in our civil rights movement; indeed, they are more alive than ever before. Whether expressed in a sit-in at lunch counters, a freedom ride into Mississippi, a peaceful protest in Albany, Georgia, a bus boycott in Montgomery, Alabama, these are outgrowths of Thoreau’s insistence that evil must be resisted and that no moral man can patiently adjust to injustice.

reply.author: BryanCaplan
reply.content: @hdthoreau’s advice is again sound. Don’t work for the IRS, never support higher taxes on anything, and never let anyone pretend that you pay taxes of your own free will. Taxation is always theft, and the more people hear this insight repeated, the sooner they’ll see taxation for what it is.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: If I devote myself to other pursuits and contemplations, I must first see, at least, that I do not pursue them sitting upon another man’s shoulders. I must get off him first, that he may pursue his contemplations too.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: It would be worth the while to ask ourselves weekly, Is our life innocent enough? Do we live inhumanely, toward man or beast, in thought or act? To be serene and successful we must be at one with the universe. The least conscious and needless injury inflicted on any creature is to its extent a suicide. What peace—or life—can a murderer have?

post.author: thoreau
post.content: See what gross inconsistency is tolerated. I have heard some of my townsmen say, “I should like to have them order me out to help put down an insurrection of the slaves, or to march to Mexico,—see if I would go;" and yet these very men have each, directly by their allegiance, and so indirectly, at least, by their money, furnished a substitute.

reply.author: emerson
reply.content: We live in a very low state of the world, and pay unwilling tribute to governments founded on force.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: The soldier is applauded who refuses to serve in an unjust war by those who do not refuse to sustain the unjust government which makes the war; is applauded by those whose own act and authority he disregards and sets at nought; as if the State were penitent to that degree that it hired one to scourge it while it sinned, but not to that degree that it left off sinning for a moment.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Thus, under the name of order and civil government, we are all made at last to pay homage to and support our own meanness. After the first blush of sin comes its indifference; and from immoral it becomes, as it were, unmoral, and not quite unnecessary to that life which we have made.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: The broadest and most prevalent error requires the most disinterested virtue to sustain it. The slight reproach to which the virtue of patriotism is commonly liable, the noble are most likely to incur.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Those who, while they disapprove of the character and measures of a government, yield to it their allegiance and support, are undoubtedly its most conscientious supporters, and so frequently the most serious obstacles to reform.

reply.author: AJMuste
reply.content: The very fact that you are ordinarily a law-abiding and conscientious person actually makes your influence for perpetuating this evil greater.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Some are petitioning the State to dissolve the Union, to disregard the requisitions of the President. Why do they not dissolve it themselves,—the union between themselves and the State,—and refuse to pay their quota into its treasury? Do not they stand in the same relation to the State, that the State does to the Union? And have not the same reasons prevented the State from resisting the Union, which have prevented them from resisting the State?

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: My advice to the State is simply this: to dissolve her union with the slaveholder instantly. She can find no respectable law or precedent which sanctions its continuance. And to each inhabitant of Massachusetts, to dissolve his union with the State, as long as she hesitates to do her duty.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: How can a man be satisfied to entertain an opinion merely, and enjoy it? Is there any enjoyment in it, if his opinion is that he is aggrieved? If you are cheated out of a single dollar by your neighbor, you do not rest satisfied with knowing that you are cheated, or with saying that you are cheated, or even with petitioning him to pay you your due; but you take effectual steps at once to obtain the full amount, and see that you are never cheated again.

reply.author: georgewoodcock
reply.content: We do not develop principles merely for the luxury of enjoying their possession. To give them meaning we must act in accordance with them, no matter how we may offend the law or public opinion.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Action from principle,—the perception and the performance of right,—changes things and relations; it is essentially revolutionary, and does not consist wholly with any thing which was. It not only divides states and churches, it divides families; aye, it divides the individual, separating the diabolical in him from the divine.

reply.author: heinzeulau
reply.content: “Action from principle,” with its insistence on ends, if shorn of metaphysics, appears as little more than the old and familiar doctrine that the end justifies the means.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: I do not complain of any tactics that are effective of good, whether one wields the quill or the sword, but I shall not think him mistaken who quickest succeeds to liberate the slave. I will judge of the tactics by the fruits.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Unjust laws exist: shall we be content to obey them, or shall we endeavor to amend them, and obey them until we have succeeded, or shall we transgress them at once?

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Men generally, under such a government as this, think that they ought to wait until they have persuaded the majority to alter them. They think that, if they should resist, the remedy would be worse than the evil. But it is the fault of the government itself that the remedy is worse than the evil. It makes it worse.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: Why is it not more apt to anticipate and provide for reform? Why does it not cherish its wise minority? Why does it cry and resist before it is hurt? Why does it not encourage its citizens to be on the alert to point out its faults, and do better than it would have them? Why does it always crucify Christ and excommunicate Copernicus and Luther, and pronounce Washington and Franklin rebels?

reply.author: williampaley
reply.content: That people, government, and constitution, is the freest, which makes the best provision for the enacting of expedient and salutary laws.

reply.author: HarryVJaffa
reply.content: To cherish a wise minority is, in substance, what representative government is supposed to do. But why should a self-appointed wise minority, outside of government, be entitled to an obedience denied by @hdthoreau to the minority chosen constitutionally by the majority? Thoreau’s strictures against law and constitutional majority rule can only lead not to rule by a “wise minority” but to lawless tyranny.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: Pray, is virtue constitutional, or vice? Is equity constitutional, or iniquity? It is as impertinent, in important moral and vital questions like this, to ask whether a law is constitutional or not, as to ask whether it is profitable or not. Sir, the question is not whether you or your grandfather, seventy years ago, entered into an agreement to serve the devil, and that service is not accordingly now due; but whether you will not now, for once and last, serve God—in spite of your own past recreancy or that of your ancestors—and obey that eternal and only just Constitution which he, and not any Jefferson or Adams, has written in your being.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: We talk about a representative government, but what a monster of a government is that where the noblest faculties of the mind, & the whole heart, are not represented. A semi-human tiger or ox stalking over the earth, with its heart taken out & the top of its brain shot away.

link.title: Nicolaus Copernicus
link.description: Renaissance polymath who pioneered a heliocentric model of the solar system

link.title: Martin Luther
link.description: The seminal figure of the Protestant Reformation, whose theological beliefs form the basis of Lutheranism

post.author: thoreau
post.content: One would think, that a deliberate and practical denial of its authority was the only offense never contemplated by government; else, why has it not assigned its definite, its suitable and proportionate penalty? If a man who has no property refuses but once to earn nine shillings for the State, he is put in prison for a period unlimited by any law that I know, and determined only by the discretion of those who placed him there; but if he should steal ninety times nine shillings from the State, he is soon permitted to go at large again.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: If the injustice is part of the necessary friction of the machine of government, let it go, let it go: perchance it will wear smooth,—certainly the machine will wear out. If the injustice has a spring, or a pulley, or a rope, or a crank, exclusively for itself, then perhaps you may consider whether the remedy will not be worse than the evil; but if it is of such a nature that it requires you to be the agent of injustice to another, then, I say, break the law. Let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine.

reply.author: williampaley
reply.content: It may be as much a duty, at one time, to resist government, as it is, at another, to obey it; to wit, whenever more advantage will, in our opinion, accrue to the community from resistance than mischief.

reply.author: emerson
reply.content: Every actual State is corrupt. Good men must not obey the laws too well.

reply.author: GilbertSeldes
reply.content: @hdthoreau’s withdrawal from the social state is entirely a matter of morals, and it is natural enough for him to speak so and to act so; nevertheless, it was accidental. In most of his contacts with the law, his withers were unwrung and he said with some acerbity, let the galled jade wince; he has other business in life, business more interesting than the destruction of the State to which he is, for the most part, not hostile, but indifferent.

reply.author: WalterHarding
reply.content: Civil disobedience is a sort of non-violent sabotage wherein the conscientious citizen drags his heels on the wagon of a government hell-bent for destruction. That it is effective out of all proportion to its weight may be ascribed to the fact that it places the burden of action upon the opponent.

reply.author: mariosavio
reply.content: There’s a time when the operation of the machine becomes so odious, makes you so sick at heart that you can’t take part! You can’t even passively take part! And you’ve got to put your bodies upon the gears and upon the wheels, upon the levers, upon all the apparatus—and you’ve got to make it stop! And you’ve got to indicate to the people who run it, to the people who own it—that unless you’re free the machine will be prevented from working at all!!

reply.author: arendt
reply.content: You’re right: individual conscience requires nothing more. Conscience is unpolitical.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: What I have to do is to see, at any rate, that I do not lend myself to the wrong which I condemn.

reply.author: thoreau
reply.content: While the law holds fast the thief and murderer, it lets itself go loose. When I have not paid the tax which the state demanded for that protection which I did not want, itself has robbed me; when I have asserted the liberty it presumed to declare, itself has imprisoned me. Poor creature! if it knows no better I will not blame it. If it cannot live but by these means, I can. I do not wish, it happens, to be associated with Massachusetts, either in holding slaves or in conquering Mexico. I am a little better than herself in these respects.

reply.author: king
reply.content: I was moved when I first read this work. I became convinced that what we were preparing to do in Montgomery was related to what @hdthoreau expressed. We were simply saying to the white community, “We can no longer lend our cooperation to an evil system.”

reply.author: HerbertJStoring
reply.content: The nexus of taxes connects every man with every wrong (as well as every right) done by the state. And if a man pays no tax, he would still be connected by commerce or civil intercourse. If the lesson of civil disobedience is to become in no way the agent of injustice, the result is revolution against this government, both in @hdthoreau’s time and ours, and against every government I have read of or heard of.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: As for adopting the ways which the State has provided for remedying the evil, I know not of such ways. They take too much time, and a man’s life will be gone. I have other affairs to attend to.

reply.author: king
reply.content: I have yet to engage in a direct action campaign that was “well timed” in the view of those who have not suffered. For years now I have heard the word “Wait!” It rings in the ear of every Negro with piercing familiarity. This “Wait” has almost always meant “Never.”

post.author: thoreau
post.content: I came into this world, not chiefly to make this a good place to live in, but to live in it, be it good or bad. A man has not every thing to do, but something; and because he cannot do every thing, it is not necessary that he should do something wrong.

post.author: thoreau
post.content: It is not my business to be petitioning the governor or the legislature any more than it is theirs to petition me; and, if they should not hear my petition, what should I do then? But in this case the State has provided no way: its very Constitution is the evil. This may seem to be harsh and stubborn and unconciliatory; but it is to treat with the utmost kindness and consideration the only spirit that can appreciate or deserves it. So is all change for the better, like birth and death which convulse the body.

reply.author: hugobedau
reply.content: Why is this not your business, indeed the first order of business of anyone who disagrees with the majority?

link.title: Constitution of Massachusetts
link.description: The fundamental governing document of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts

post.author: thoreau
